title: US-Indian Space Mission Maps Extreme Subsidence in Mexico City
key_claim: NISAR mission (NASA-ISRO L-band SAR, launched July 2025) mapped parts of Mexico City subsiding by more than 2 cm/month between October 2025 and January 2026; parts of the metropolitan area have been sinking around 35 cm/year since the 1990s, damaging metro, water lines and buildings; NISAR collects data twice every 12 days, enabling near-real-time monitoring across the globe.
notes: Primary government source - the technology inflection making subsidence visible at monthly granularity.

title: Underestimation of present-day sea levels reveals greater coastal flood risk globally
key_claim: Tidal-gauge analysis finds actual sea levels are 9.4-10.6 inches higher on average than standard model estimates; in 385 cases examined the model-derived sea levels were 3 feet or more off; around 80 million people are today living on land in coastal areas below sea level - almost twice previous estimates.
notes: Peer-reviewed primary research recalibrating the baseline coastal flood-risk geography.

title: Land subsidence in the world's river deltas
key_claim: Satellite-radar 3D maps of 40 of the world's biggest river deltas; subsidence afflicts more than half of them; in 18 cases subsidence rates exceed those of rising tides - more than doubling the effective yearly rise in local sea levels, and in some cases multiplying it tenfold; deltas affected include the Nile, Mekong, Mahanadi (India), and Yellow River (China).
notes: Peer-reviewed primary research with high spatial resolution for the first time.

publisher: Nature Sustainability (Sadhasivam, Ohenhen, Khorrami, Werth, Shirzaei)
title: Building damage risk in sinking Indian megacities
key_claim: Satellite radar 2015-23 across Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru; 878 sq km sinking; 1.9 million people exposed to >4 mm/yr; 2,406 structures in New Delhi/Mumbai/Chennai at high damage risk now; up to 23,529 buildings at very high risk over 50 years if trends persist.
notes: Structural anchor - canonical primary research for the Indian megacity building-damage quantification.

title: A More Troubling Picture of Sea Level Rise Comes Into View
key_claim: Two major 2026 Nature studies (Seeger-Minderhoud sea-level baseline; Ohenhen delta subsidence) jointly conclude that 'impacts of sea level rise under climate change have been systematically underestimated' (Matt Palmer, UK Met Office); 'we are seeing an emerging body of research that rewrites the story of coastal vulnerability' (Franck Ghomsi, University of Cape Town).
notes: Authoritative environmental journalism synthesising the two primary studies, with expert quotes.

title: Sinking Cities: Hydrogeological Drivers, Urban Vulnerability, and Sustainable Management Pathways
key_claim: Systematic literature review of 167 peer-reviewed studies (1969-2026) on urban subsidence; subsidence affects more than 1.6 billion people globally; groundwater withdrawal is the dominant control mechanism, lowering pore pressure and driving consolidation; Asia's coastal megacities show strongly clustered subsidence hotspots.
notes: Academic synthesis review establishing the global scale and mechanism.

title: One of the planet's biggest cities is sinking so rapidly it's visible from space
key_claim: Mexico City (population ~22 million) sits atop an aquifer providing ~60% of drinking water; new NISAR data show parts subsiding ~0.8 inches/month (>9.5 inches/year); Indonesia is relocating its capital from Jakarta to a new island due to subsidence and flooding.
notes: Mainstream business/news framing of the Mexico City story for executive readership.

title: How 'sinking cities' can address subsidence challenges
key_claim: WEF framing of municipal adaptation pathways for sinking cities including Jakarta, Tokyo, Shanghai.
notes: Excluded from final scan due to age - kept here as reference.
